title: A loop is a conveyor belt

beats.say: How does a loop know where it is, and when to stop? Picture a sushi conveyor belt.
A list is like the whole menu printed on paper. You can read it again and again. To loop, Python asks for a belt, called an iterator. It is a helper that remembers your place.
Each time the loop asks for the next plate, the belt hands over one and moves on. When the belt is empty, it shouts stop. That signal is named StopIteration. The loop hears it and quietly ends.
Here is the catch. Plates you have eaten are gone. A file or a generator is a belt, so a second loop over it sees nothing. A list is a menu, so you can loop all day.

check.q: You loop over a file once, then loop over the same file object again. What happens in the second loop?
opts: It starts again from the first line
It does nothing, because the file is already used up
It raises an error right away
check.why: A file is its own iterator, like a belt. After one full pass it is at the end, so the second loop gets StopIteration at once and runs zero times, with no error.

work: Next time you loop twice over the same thing, ask: is it a list or a one-shot belt?
Check which of your data sources are files or generators rather than lists.

title: iter and next, step by step

beats.say: What is a for loop actually doing behind your back?
First, Python calls iter on your data. That returns an iterator, an object that tracks its position. Then it calls next again and again. Each call returns one value, like ten, then twenty.
When values run out, next raises StopIteration. The loop catches it and breaks out. No error reaches you.
Try it by hand with iter of a list holding ten and twenty. Next gives ten. Next gives twenty. The third next raises StopIteration. Two items, three calls.

show.title: By hand
show.text:
it = iter([10, 20])
next(it)  # 10
next(it)  # 20
next(it)  # StopIteration

beats.say: Iter on a list makes a fresh iterator each time, so lists loop many times. Iter on a file returns the file itself, so it is spent after one pass.

chip.text: Iterator is spent after one pass

check.q: For it = iter([10, 20]), what does the third call to next(it) do?
opts: Returns None
Returns 10 again
Raises StopIteration
check.why: After two values the iterator is exhausted. The next call raises StopIteration, which is the signal a for loop uses to end.

work: Open a Python shell and step through iter and next on a list, then on a generator.
Read a loop you wrote and write out the iter and next calls it implies.

title: The silent empty second pass

beats.say: Why does your second pass over a file give you nothing, with no error?

A file or generator is its own iterator. Calling iter on it returns itself, with the same position. After the first loop, that position is the end. The second loop gets StopIteration on the very first next, so it runs zero times, silently.
This bites in pipelines. Say you count rows, then loop again to write them. The count works, the write sees zero rows, and your output file is empty. No crash, no warning.

Fixes: rebuild the generator or reopen the file for each pass, do everything in one pass, or load into a list if it fits in memory. Also, calling next by hand on an empty iterator raises StopIteration, so pass a default.

show.title: Safe patterns
items: Rebuild or reopen for each pass
Do all work in one pass
Use a list if it fits in memory

check.q: A generator is looped once to count rows, then looped again to write them. The output file is empty. Why?
opts: The generator was exhausted by the first loop
Writing to files is lazy and was skipped
The count loop corrupted the data
check.why: A generator is its own iterator and is consumed by the first pass. The second loop gets StopIteration immediately and writes nothing, without raising an error.

work: Add a test that asserts row counts after each stage, so empty second passes are caught.
Grep your code for generators or file objects used in more than one loop.

title: One-shot iterators: cost and trade-offs

beats.say: When should you refuse to use a list, and when is a one-shot iterator a trap?
A list of one hundred million rows at about one hundred bytes each needs ten gigabytes of memory. An iterator holds one row at a time, so memory stays flat, whatever the file size.
The price: one pass only, no length, no jumping back. Two consumers can't share one iterator without stealing each other's rows.

So design for single pass. Do filter, transform and aggregate in one chain. If several steps need the data, either read the source again, which is cheap for files and costly for APIs, or write an intermediate result to disk such as Parquet.
Use a list when data is small and reused. Use iterators when it is big or streaming.

show.title: Choose
items: Many readers: persist to disk first

check.q: Three steps each need the full output of an expensive API crawl that is too big for memory. What is the best design?
opts: Pass one generator to all three steps
Write the crawl to disk once, then let each step read it
Re-crawl the API for each step
check.why: One generator would be consumed by the first step. Re-crawling is slow and costly. Persisting once, for example as Parquet, keeps memory flat and lets each step read independently.

work: Estimate row count times row size before choosing a list for any dataset.
Document which pipeline stages are single-pass and who consumes them.
Persist expensive intermediate results when more than one consumer needs them.

title: A river you can't rewind

beats.say: Ever tried to rewind a river?
A generator is like a river. Water flows past you once. You can count what went by, but then it is gone.
A list is like a bucket. You scoop the water in once. Then you can look, count, and pour it as often as you like.
Here is the trap. You count the river first, then ask for the fares, and find a dry riverbed. Nothing crashes. You just quietly get nothing.
The fix is simple. Fill a bucket if it fits. Or walk back to the spring and start the river again.

show.title: Two fixes
items: Fill a bucket: make a list if it fits
Walk back to the spring: restart from the source

check.q: You count a generator's items, then try to read them again. What do you most likely get?
opts: The same items again
An error that stops the program
Nothing, with no error
Only the first item
check.why: The generator is already used up after the first pass, so the second pass finds nothing and raises no error.

work: Look for any variable holding a generator that is used in two places.
Ask yourself whether each data source is a river or a bucket before you reuse it.

title: Why the second pass is empty

beats.say: Why does the second line of this code return an empty list?

show.title: The trap
show.text:
rows = (parse(l) for l in open('trips.csv'))
n = sum(1 for _ in rows)
fares = [r['fare'] for r in rows]

beats.say: A generator keeps one pointer into its source. Each time you ask for a next item, the pointer moves forward. It never moves back.
Say trips dot csv has ten million rows. Sum over the generator walks the pointer to the end. Ten million rows are read, and the pointer now sits at the finish.
The next loop asks for a row and gets told the stream is finished straight away. No error, just an empty list.
So either call list once, if it fits in memory, or build a fresh generator from the file for the second pass.

show.title: Two ways out
items: Call list once, if it fits in memory
Build a fresh generator for each pass

check.q: After sum consumes a generator, what is the state of that generator?
opts: Reset to the first item
Exhausted, so loops end at once
Holding a copy of all rows
Raising an error on every next call
check.why: The pointer sits at the end, so any new loop finishes straight away without error or items.

work: When you need two passes, write a small function that opens the file and returns a fresh generator.
Test with a tiny file and assert the second result is not empty.

title: Gotchas of one-shot iterables

beats.say: Why can len on a generator never work?
A generator does not know its size. It makes each item only when asked, so the count exists only after you have walked it all. Walking it uses it up.

Worse, a function that takes any iterable may quietly loop twice. Say it checks for empty, then processes. With a list that works. With a generator, the check eats the first row, or the second loop sees nothing.
Also beware itertools tee, which splits one stream into copies. It buffers every item one copy has read and the other has not, so memory can balloon.
Rule: loop once, or state clearly that you need two passes, or take a list.

show.title: The rule
items: Or say clearly that you need two passes

check.q: A function receives an iterable, checks whether it is empty by reading one item, then loops over it. What goes wrong with a generator?
opts: Nothing, the check is free
The check consumes the first row
It raises a type error
It copies the data to disk
check.why: Reading one item advances the pointer for good, so that row is lost to the later loop.

work: Review functions that accept an iterable and flag any that loop twice.
Document in the docstring whether a function needs one pass or many.

title: Replay, store or single pass

beats.say: When is rerunning the source better than storing the data?
Materialising with list costs memory. Ten million rows of dicts can take several gigabytes. If it exceeds RAM, the job dies, so list is only safe when you know the size is bounded.
Restarting costs time. Reading the file twice doubles the input and parsing work, and a network stream or database cursor may not be replayable at all.
Better still, use one pass. Compute the count and the fares together, keeping running totals. Constant memory, one read.
If you truly need many passes, write to Parquet once, or load into DuckDB, and query it repeatedly from disk.

check.q: You need a count and a fare average from a file far larger than RAM. What is the best design?
opts: Call list on the generator
Make two generators and read the file twice
Compute both in one pass with running totals
Call len on the generator
check.why: One pass with running totals keeps memory constant and reads the data only once.

work: Rewrite two-pass jobs as one pass with accumulators where you can.
For repeated analysis of big data, land it once in Parquet and query it with DuckDB.
Check whether your source can be replayed before choosing to restart.

title: Batching is carrying more per trip

beats.say: Would you carry groceries from the car to the kitchen one item at a time?
Of course not. The walk takes the same time whether you hold one tin or five bags. That walk is the fixed cost of every trip.

Databases work the same way. Every insert is a trip across the network, with waiting at both ends. Sending one thousand rows in one trip beats one thousand trips. Grouping items like this is called batching.
But a bag can get too heavy. Too big, and you strain, or drop everything. And the last bag is often half empty. Still carry it, or those items stay in the car.

show.title: Two things to watch
items: Too heavy a bag: a failure costs everything
The last half-empty bag still has to go

check.q: Why is sending 1,000 rows in one insert faster than 1,000 single inserts?
opts: Each row is smaller when grouped
You pay the fixed cost of the trip once, not 1,000 times
The database skips checking the data
check.why: Each call carries a fixed cost, such as network wait and setup. Batching shares that cost across many rows.

work: List the loops in your code that call a database or API once per row.
Pick one and ask: could it send a group of rows in one call?

title: How a chunking generator works

beats.say: How do you send ten million rows to a database without loading them all, or sending them one by one?

show.sub: too many to hold, too slow one by one

beats.say: Say each insert costs five milliseconds of round trip, and the row itself takes almost nothing. One thousand single inserts cost five seconds. One insert of one thousand rows costs about five milliseconds plus a little. That is the saving.
A chunking function does it. It reads items from the source, adds each to a buffer, and when the buffer reaches the size, it yields the buffer and starts a new one.
Memory stays flat, because only one buffer exists at a time. Ten million rows at a thousand per batch means ten thousand inserts.

check.q: You load 10 million rows with a chunk size of 1,000. How many insert calls do you make, and how much data is held in memory?
opts: 10,000 calls, about 1,000 rows in memory
10 million calls, 1 row in memory
10,000 calls, all 10 million rows in memory
check.why: The generator holds one buffer at a time, so memory stays at roughly one batch while you make 10,000 calls.

work: Write a chunked helper and run it on a lazy source, such as a file reader.
Time 1,000 single inserts against one batch of 1,000 on your own database.

title: Chunking gotchas that bite

beats.say: Your batch loader ran clean, but the last forty rows never arrived. What happened?
The loop only yields when the buffer is full. With 10,040 rows and a size of 1,000, the final 40 sit in the buffer when the loop ends. After the loop, you must yield whatever is left.

show.title: The easy-to-forget line

beats.say: Another trap is reusing the buffer. If you clear the list instead of making a new one, anything still holding the old batch sees it change under its feet. Make a fresh list each time.
And when a batch fails, you retry all of it. So the insert must be safe to repeat, for example an upsert by key, or you get duplicates.

show.title: Retry the whole batch
items: A failure repeats every row in the batch
Use upserts or unique keys so repeats are harmless

check.q: A chunker yields only inside the loop when len(buf) equals size. What goes wrong with 10,040 rows and size 1,000?
opts: It crashes at row 10,000
The last 40 rows are silently dropped
The first batch is too large
check.why: The final partial buffer is never full, so it is never yielded unless you add a check after the loop.

work: Add a test with a row count that is not a multiple of the batch size.
Make your batch writes idempotent, with an upsert or a unique key.

title: Choosing batch size as an architect

beats.say: Is bigger always better when you batch? No, and the cost shows up in three places.

Bigger batches mean fewer round trips, but more memory, longer locks, and a bigger retry when one fails. Rows vary in size, so cap by bytes, not only row count. Start with five hundred to five thousand rows, or a few megabytes, then measure.
For files, aim near one hundred twenty-eight megabytes. Ten thousand tiny Parquet files make every query slow, because opening each file costs more than reading it.
In streams, batching adds waiting. Flush on size or on a timer, whichever comes first, so a quiet trickle is not stuck. And skip batching when you need each result immediately.

show.title: Flush rules
items: Flush when full or when the timer fires
Skip batching when each result is needed at once
Measure throughput and p99 latency before settling

check.q: A stream sends only a few events per minute into a batch of 5,000. What should you add?
opts: A bigger batch size
A time-based flush
Fewer retries
check.why: Without a timer, events wait until the batch fills, which may take hours. Flushing on size or time bounds the delay.

work: Cap batches by bytes as well as rows, then load-test a few sizes.
Add a time-based flush to any streaming writer, and compact small files on a schedule.

title: The dish line that never piles up

beats.say: How do you wash a million dishes in a kitchen with room for only three?
You build an assembly line. One helper fetches a plate, one scrubs, one dries, one stacks. Each plate goes through every helper before the next plate is fetched.

show.title: One plate at a time down the *line*

beats.say: Nothing moves until the last helper asks for a plate. That request travels back down the line to the pantry. So the counter only ever holds a few plates, whether there are ten dishes or ten million.

chip.text: Only a few plates at once

beats.say: In Python, each helper is a generator. That is a function that hands out one item, then pauses until asked again. Chain small generators together, each doing one job, and you can process data far bigger than memory.

show.title: Generator pipeline
items: Generator: hands out one item, then pauses
Each stage does one small job
Memory stays flat at any size

check.q: In the dish line, when does the first helper fetch a plate?
opts: Immediately, to fill the counter
Only when the last helper asks for one
After all dishes are counted
When the counter is full
check.why: Work is pulled from the end of the line. Nothing is fetched until the last stage asks, which keeps the counter nearly empty.

work: Think of one job where you load a whole file into a list, and picture it as a line of single-item helpers instead.
Write down which of your scripts would break if the input grew ten times larger.

title: Filter and load fifty million rows

beats.say: A trips file has fifty million lines. How does Python filter and load it using almost no memory?

You chain generators. Read lines yields one line. Parse turns it into a dictionary. Only completed keeps rows whose status is completed. Building this chain runs nothing. It only wires the stages together.

Work starts when the loop asks for a batch. Chunked pulls from only completed, which pulls from parse, which pulls from the reader. One row flows through every stage before the next row is read. Chunked collects one thousand rows, then write batch sends them to the database in one call.
Memory holds one line plus one batch of a thousand rows. Fifty million lines or five hundred million, the footprint is the same.

check.q: Which line makes the pipeline actually start reading the file?
opts: Calling read_lines on the file
Wrapping stages inside each other
The for loop over chunked that asks for a batch
Defining the parse function
check.why: Generators are lazy. Wiring them runs nothing. The for loop asking for the next batch pulls rows through every stage.

work: Replace a read-all-then-loop script with a chain of generators and compare peak memory.
Pick a batch size by testing database write time at 500, 1000 and 5000 rows.

title: Lazy like Spark, endless like Kafka

beats.say: What do a Python generator pipeline and a Spark job have in common?

Both are lazy. Spark transformations like filter and map only build a plan. Nothing runs until an action such as count or write pulls data through it. Generators work the same way. The last stage asks, and everything upstream responds.
A Kafka consumer loop is the same shape with an endless source. It pulls a message, handles it, and pulls the next, so memory stays flat forever.
To read many files as one stream, use yield from. It hands out everything another generator produces, so a loop over a list of daily files looks like one long file to the next stage.

show.title: Many files, one stream

check.q: What does yield from do in a pipeline?
opts: Runs several generators in parallel
Hands out every item another generator produces, as one stream
Loads that generator's output into a list
Restarts the generator when it ends
check.why: It forwards each item from another generator one at a time, so many files look like one stream without building a list.

work: Write an all_lines generator that chains daily files into one stream.
Explain in one sentence which Spark calls are transformations and which are actions in a job you own.

title: Why the pipeline ran dry

beats.say: You loop over the same pipeline twice, and the second loop writes nothing. Why?
A generator is single use. Each value is handed out once, then gone. After the first pass it is exhausted, and asking again gives nothing, with no error. To rerun, build a fresh pipeline.

Errors also surface late. One malformed line makes parse raise, and the exception kills the generator for good, since it cannot resume. Catch bad lines inside parse and send them to a reject file, so one bad row does not stop fifty million good ones.

Two more gotchas. Chunked must flush the last partial batch, or you lose up to nine hundred ninety nine rows. And open the file in a with block inside the reader, so it closes even if the pipeline stops early.

show.title: Two more traps
items: Open files with a with block in the reader
Debugging with list consumes the rows

check.q: A parse stage raises on line 7 million and you did not catch it. What happens?
opts: Parse skips that row and continues
The exception propagates and the generator cannot resume
The pipeline restarts from the first line
Only that batch is dropped
check.why: An uncaught exception ends the generator permanently. Handle bad rows inside the stage and route them to a reject file.

work: Add a reject file path to your parse stage and count rejected rows.
Test your chunked function with a row count that is not a multiple of the batch size.
Never call list on a live pipeline while debugging; use itertools islice to peek at a fresh copy.

title: When generators stop being enough

beats.say: At what point should you stop writing generator pipelines and reach for Spark?

A generator pipeline is one thread on one machine. Pure Python parses maybe two hundred thousand rows a second, so fifty million rows take about four minutes. That is fine for a nightly job. At five billion rows it is seven hours, and you cannot split the work across machines.

show.title: Run time at 200k rows per second

beats.say: It also handles only row by row work. Sorting, joins and group bys need to see many rows at once, so a streaming pipeline cannot do them without spilling to disk. For those, pick DuckDB or Polars on one big machine, or Spark when data outgrows it.
Keep generators for simple streaming loads, and make writes idempotent so a failed batch can be retried safely. Bigger batches mean fewer round trips but more to redo on failure.

show.title: Design rules
items: Idempotent writes so retries are safe
Batch size: round trips versus redo cost

check.q: Which job is the worst fit for a plain generator pipeline?
opts: Filtering a huge CSV and loading it in batches
Sorting five billion rows and joining them to another large table
Streaming Kafka messages into a database
Combining daily files into one stream
check.why: Sorts and joins need many rows at once and benefit from parallelism, so use DuckDB, Polars or Spark instead of a single-thread streaming pipeline.

work: Measure rows per second of your slowest stage before deciding whether to scale out.
Make your batch writes idempotent, for example with upserts keyed on trip id.
Write down the row count at which your job misses its deadline; that is your trigger to move to Spark.

title: A conveyor belt of parcels

beats.say: How do you look at the first five items on a belt that never ends, without unloading the whole thing?
Picture a conveyor belt of parcels. A tool called islice grabs the first five, then stops the belt. The rest is never touched, even if a billion parcels are waiting.
Chain joins two belts end to end, so they act like one long belt. It is the same idea as union all in a database.

Groupby makes piles, but only of neighbours. Three red parcels in a row make one pile. A blue one, then red again, starts a brand new red pile. So shuffled colours give many small piles. Sort first if you want one pile per colour.

chip.text: Sort first for one pile per colour

check.q: A belt of parcels has colours red, red, blue, red. How many piles does groupby make?
opts: Two, one red and one blue
Three, because the last red is not next to the first reds
Four, one per parcel
check.why: Groupby only joins neighbours with the same key. Red, red is one pile, blue is another, and the final red starts a new pile, making three.

work: Next time you need first N rows to inspect a big file, use islice instead of loading a list.
Before using groupby, ask yourself whether equal keys are guaranteed to sit next to each other.

title: Lazy tools, flat memory

beats.say: A file has fifty million rows. How do you take the first five, add up running totals, and never load the file?
These tools are lazy. Islice of rows, five, pulls exactly five items from the source, then stops. Memory stays flat, and the file is read only as far as row five.
Accumulate turns one, two, three into one, three, six, a running total, one value at a time. Count starts at one and counts up forever, so always pair it with islice or a break.
Chain takes several files and yields their rows in order, one file after another. Still nothing is loaded up front.

check.q: Why must count(1) be paired with islice or a break?
opts: It is lazy and never ends on its own
It loads every number into memory first
It only works on sorted data
check.why: Count yields numbers forever, one at a time. Without something that stops the loop, it runs endlessly.

work: Replace head-of-file list slicing with islice so you do not load the file.
Use chain over a list of file readers to process many files as one stream.

title: The groupby trap

beats.say: Why does groupby on city return Paris three times?

Because groupby only merges consecutive equal keys. It compares each row to the one just before it. Paris, Paris, Rome, Paris gives three groups, not two. SQL group by sees all rows at once. Groupby cannot, because it streams.
Second trap: each group is a live view of the same stream. Move to the next group and the old one is gone. Turn it into a list or consume it before moving on.

show.title: Groups are live views
items: Advancing the loop kills the old group
Use list of group, or consume it inside the loop

beats.say: The fix for true grouping is sorting first, which needs all data in memory or on disk, or a dict of counters. But the consecutive behaviour is useful for runs, like an online streak or a user session.

show.title: Choose on purpose
items: True group by: sort first, or use a dict
Runs and streaks: groupby is perfect
Sessions: consecutive events by one user

check.q: You saved groups from groupby into a list of the group objects, then looped over them afterwards. What do you most likely see?
opts: Every group is full and correct
The groups are empty or wrong, because the stream moved on
Python raises a sorting error
check.why: Each group shares the underlying iterator. Once the outer loop advances, earlier groups are exhausted. Materialise each group with list while you are still on it.

work: Add a sort or a dict whenever you mean SQL group by.
Wrap each group in list or sum it inside the loop, never after.
Use groupby on purpose for streaks and sessions.

title: When itertools is not enough

beats.say: When is a lazy Python pipeline the wrong tool?

show.text: When is lazy Python not enough?

beats.say: Itertools is great for one pass over a stream on one machine. It uses almost no memory and it is simple to test. But it runs on one core, and python loops handle roughly a million rows a second at best.
Real group by across a huge dataset needs sorting or hashing, so use a database, DuckDB, or Spark, which spill to disk and run in parallel. Do not hand sort fifty gigabytes in Python.

show.title: Hand the *heavy* work to an engine

beats.say: Keep itertools for glue: sampling, batching, stitching files, and detecting runs. Once you need joins, many keys, or retries, move to an engine.

show.title: Rule of thumb
items: Itertools: sample, batch, stitch, find runs
Engine: joins, wide group by, big sorts
Switch when one core or one pass breaks

check.q: You must count orders per customer across 50 GB of unsorted files. What is the best choice?
opts: Sort in Python, then use groupby
Use an engine like DuckDB or Spark that hashes and spills
Use accumulate over the files
check.why: True group by needs hashing or sorting at scale. An engine does it in parallel and spills to disk, while Python sorting is slow, single-core and memory hungry.

work: Document which pipelines are single-pass glue and which should move to an engine.
Benchmark rows per second on a sample before committing to a pure Python design.

title: A function that keeps its place

beats.say: How can a program read a file bigger than your computer's memory? Picture a friend reading you a long novel aloud.
They don't memorize the whole book first. They read one line, stop, and keep a finger on the page. Ask for the next line, and they carry on from that finger.
A generator is exactly that. It's a function that hands you one piece, then pauses, remembering where it was.
So you only ever hold one line at a time. A billion lines, or an endless stream, costs almost nothing. Compare that with copying the whole book out by hand before you start.

check.q: What makes a generator able to handle a file bigger than memory?
opts: It compresses the file
It hands out one piece at a time and pauses between them
It reads the whole file faster
check.why: A generator keeps only the current item and its place, so memory stays tiny however long the data is.

work: Think of one job that loads a whole file and ask whether one line at a time would do.
Explain generators to a teammate using the finger-on-the-page picture.

title: How yield pauses and resumes

beats.say: What actually happens when you call a function that contains yield? Nothing runs at all.
The call just returns a generator object. Each next runs the body up to the next yield, hands back that value, and pauses with every local variable kept.
The first next prints opening and returns line one. The second returns line two. The file is not reopened, and nothing is reread.
Memory is the point. A list of a hundred million squares takes gigabytes. The same thing in round brackets builds nothing until consumed, so sum over it runs in constant memory.

check.q: After g = read_lines('trips.log'), which is true?
opts: The file is open and line 1 is read
Nothing has run yet; the body starts at the first next
The whole file is loaded into a list
check.why: Calling a generator function only creates the generator object. The body runs on the first next.

work: Replace a list comprehension feeding sum or max with a generator expression.
Add a print inside a small generator to see exactly when it runs.

title: Generator gotchas

beats.say: Why does your generator seem to do nothing, then give you nothing the second time? Generators have sharp edges.
First, laziness. The file opens at the first next, not when you call the function. So a typo in the path only fails later, far from the line that caused it.
Second, one shot. Once exhausted, a generator raises StopIteration forever. Looping over it twice gives an empty second pass. Need two passes? Call the function again.

Third, cleanup. The closed message prints only if the loop finishes. Stop early, and the with block closes the file only when the generator is closed or garbage collected. Close it explicitly, or use try finally.

show.title: Stopping early
items: Closing message skipped if you break out
with block runs on close or garbage collection
Call close, or use try finally for cleanup

check.q: You loop over the same generator twice. What does the second loop do?
opts: Restarts from the first item
Raises a file error
Produces nothing, because it is already exhausted
check.why: A generator cannot rewind. Once finished, it yields nothing more. Call the function again for a fresh one.

work: Audit pipelines for generators consumed twice, such as len followed by a loop.
Wrap resource-holding generators in try finally or contextlib closing.

title: When generators are the wrong tool

beats.say: When is a generator the wrong choice? When you need the data more than once, or need it fast.

show.sub: you pay in speed and flexibility

beats.say: Generators give constant memory, but they run one item at a time on one thread. Python overhead per item adds up. A hundred million rows through pure Python takes minutes.
Need random access, sorting, or several passes? Materialize to disk, or use a tool like DuckDB or Polars that streams in batches natively.

show.title: Choose instead
items: Several passes: write to disk, then reread
Sorting or joins: DuckDB or Polars
Parallel work: split files across workers

beats.say: If you stay with generators, yield chunks of ten thousand rows to spread the per-item cost. Remember debugging is harder, since state hides inside paused frames. Use them for one pass pipelines.

show.title: Yield batches

check.q: A job must sort 500 million rows and scan them three times. What fits best?
opts: One generator pipeline over the raw file
A list comprehension in memory
An engine like DuckDB, or an intermediate file on disk
check.why: Sorting and multiple passes need random access or reuse. A single-use generator cannot give that, so use a streaming engine or stored intermediate data.
